newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iran in petrochemical deal with international firm.
newsitem.headline: Iran in petrochemical deal with international firm.

text.p: Iran on Tuesday said it reached a $600 million agreement with a Dubai-based consortium of German and South Korean companies to build a petrochemical plant in Iran, the official Iranian news agency IRNA reported.

It quoted Sadeqh Masoumi Lari, head of the Kermanshah Petrochemical Industries Company as saying "a consortium composed of German and South Korean companies would cooperate with Iran in providing machinery and technological know-how for construction of the plant".
IRNA did not name the consortium.
Lari said the plant to be built at Kermanshah, 650 km (400 miles) west of Tehran, fell under a buy-back scheme.
"He (Lari) said that once operational the complex is expected to produce 1,000 tons of amoniac and 1,500 tons of urea fertilizer a day," IRNA said.
In August, U.S. President Bill Clinton adopted a law which penalises companies investing $40 million or more a year in the oil and gas industries of Iran and Libya.
Tehran accused Washington of behaving like a bully and European countries also criticised the unilateral U.S. move, saying it would unfairly penalise their oil companies.
The United States is waging an international campaign to isolate Tehran for its alleged involvement in terrorist acts against the West.
Iran strongly denies such charges and says Washington is bent on toppling its Islamic government.

Iran last year said it was negotiating petrochemical joint ventures with Asian and European companies in what would be the forst foreign direct investment in the country's hydrocarbon sector since the 1979 revolution.
The major OPEC producer said legislation had been prepared to allow foreign investment of up to 49 percent in $3.3 billion worth of upstream projects.
Iran has tried to break out of its isolation by seeking oil and gas deals.
In August, Iran signed a $23 billion natural gas deal with Turkey.
Last year, the Islamic republic signed a $600 million deal with France's Total to delevop the Sirri E and A offshore oil and gas fields.
